noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: practical: investigate breathing in humans, including the release of carbon dioxide and the effect of exercise

primer.text: Breathing responds to demand, and the demand is measurable. This practical counts breaths per minute at rest and straight after exercise, then asks how reliably the change can be attributed to the activity — which is where the CORMS checklist earns its keep.

lessons.title: Counting the Change
sourceHeadings: Practical: The Effect of Age on Breathing
lessons.opening: Participants of a similar age sit quietly for a minute and count their breaths — one inhale plus one exhale each. They then perform identical exercise, such as running on the spot, and count again immediately. The difference between the two counts is the change in breathing rate, and repeating across participants gives a mean worth comparing.
keyPoints: Breathing rate is counted as breaths per minute, one breath being an inhale and an exhale.
A resting count comes first, then the same exercise for everyone.
The count repeats immediately after exercise stops.
Change in breathing rate equals the after-exercise rate minus the resting rate.
Repeats across participants allow a mean to be calculated.

low.restatement: Two counts and their difference measure what exercise did to breathing.
low.analogy: A stopwatch on a car before and after a hill: the delta is the hill's cost.
low.examPointer: Write the change as a subtraction — after minus before — in method answers.

medium.restatement: Exercise raises breathing rate and depth to serve the muscles' demand.
medium.analogy: A delivery service adding vans and bigger vans when orders surge.
medium.examPointer: Give the biological reason — oxygen demand and carbon dioxide clearance — not just the observation.

check.stem: How is one breath defined for the count?

options.explanation: That pairing makes each cycle countable.
The exhale completes the cycle.
A minute holds many breaths.
Breaths are not timed to heartbeats.

check.stem: When is the after-exercise count taken?

options.explanation: Delay would let the rate drift back towards rest.
Recovery would have begun, muddying the change.
That is the resting count.
The effect would have vanished.

check.stem: What does the change in breathing rate equal?

options.text: Breathing rate after exercise minus breathing rate at rest
options.explanation: The subtraction isolates the exercise effect.
That gives a negative number for a rise.

options.text: The mean of the two rates
options.explanation: The mean hides the change instead of measuring it.

options.text: The larger of the two rates
options.explanation: The larger rate alone says nothing about the change.

check.stem: Why must every participant perform the same exercise?

options.text: So the change in breathing rate is comparable across participants
options.explanation: Identical demand makes the counts comparable.
Safety is not the comparison reason.
Counting works at any rhythm.
Practicality is not the scientific reason.

check.stem: Which conclusion follows from the change in breathing rate?

options.text: Exercise makes breathing both faster and deeper
options.explanation: Both the count per minute and the breath size rise.
The counts rise after exercise.
The change is the whole point of the practical.

options.text: Exercise only deepens breathing, not its rate
options.explanation: Both frequency and depth increase.

check.stem: State the equation for the change in breathing rate.
check.modelAnswer: Change in breathing rate equals the rate after exercise minus the rate at rest.

check.stem: Name two variables that must be kept the same across participants.
check.modelAnswer: The type and duration of exercise, and the environment such as temperature, plus the same counting method.

check.stem: Explain why the mean of several participants is better than one person's numbers.
check.modelAnswer: Because individuals differ in fitness, motivation and health, so one person's counts could be atypical; averaging across the group smooths those quirks and gives a value that reflects the exercise effect rather than one body's idiosyncrasies.

check.stem: A student counts 14 breaths per minute at rest and 30 straight after one minute of step-ups. State the change and the biological cause.
check.modelAnswer: The change is 16 breaths per minute; the cause is the muscles' extra oxygen demand and extra carbon dioxide output during the step-ups, which drove the deeper, faster breathing.

lessons.title: Limitations and Fixes
lessons.opening: Honest practicals admit their weak spots. Participant variation is hard to control; exercise effort differs between people; counting breaths is error-prone because rates shift fast; and the room itself — temperature, air quality, nerves — leaks into the numbers. Each weakness has a standard fix worth quoting.
keyPoints: Fitness, lifestyle and health vary between participants and cannot all be controlled.
Motivation and ability make exercise intensity differ between people.
Counting errors arise because breathing rate changes quickly after exercise.
A controlled exercise, such as step-ups at a set pace, pins the intensity down.
Counting for a fixed short spell and scaling up reduces the timing error.

low.restatement: Every measurement weakness has a named fix — learn them as pairs.
low.analogy: A survey with sloppy handwriting: standardise the form and the mess shrinks.
low.examPointer: Quote the limitation and its solution together; one without the other scores half.

medium.restatement: Set-pace exercise, immediate short counts, and identical indoor conditions — the three fixes.
medium.analogy: A kitchen timer strategy: measure the freshest interval and scale it to the recipe.
medium.examPointer: Write limitation then solution in the same sentence for full marks.

check.stem: Which fix addresses uneven exercise intensity?

options.text: A controlled exercise such as step-ups at a set pace
options.explanation: Standardising the effort removes the variability.
That fixes timing error, not intensity.
Age is not the intensity fix.
More data does not standardise effort.

check.stem: Why is breathing rate hard to measure accurately?

options.text: It changes quickly after exercise, so timing errors distort the count
options.explanation: The rate decays while you count it.
Breaths are visible and countable.
Cooperation is not the stated problem.
Exercise raises breathing, never stops it.

check.stem: What does multiplying a 15-second count by four give?

options.explanation: Four quarter-minutes make a minute.
The count measures frequency, not depth.
The scaled figure is the post-exercise rate.
Nothing about the count gives recovery time.

check.stem: Which is NOT a standard fix for the counting or intensity problems?

options.explanation: Music is not among the listed controls.
Indoors levels the temperature and air quality.
That is the stated levelling measure.
Rest settles everyone onto the same baseline.

check.stem: Why might two participants show different changes despite identical exercise?

options.text: Fitness, motivation and health differ between people
options.explanation: Individual physiology colours the response.
They can, imperfectly.

options.text: Because exercise always gives the same change
options.explanation: It does not; variation is the norm.
No stopwatch is involved in breath counting.

check.stem: State the solution for the timing error in breath counting.
check.modelAnswer: Begin counting immediately after exercise and count for a fixed short period, such as fifteen seconds, then multiply up to a per-minute rate.

check.stem: Name three external conditions that can influence breathing rate.
check.modelAnswer: Temperature, air quality and stress levels.

check.stem: Explain why a step-up test at a fixed pace is fairer than 'run as fast as you can'.
check.modelAnswer: Because a fixed pace gives every participant the same workload, so any difference in the breathing response reflects the person, not a private choice of effort; 'as fast as you can' lets motivation and ability silently rewrite the intensity.

check.stem: Design the control that would let a class compare smokers and non-smokers on this practical, naming one extra limitation it introduces.
check.modelAnswer: Match participants for age and fitness across both groups, hold the exercise and environment identical, and compare the mean changes; the extra limitation is that smoking history varies in amount and duration, so the groups are not perfectly matched even after controls.

glossary.definition: The number of breaths taken per minute; one breath is an inhale plus an exhale.
The practical checklist: Change, Organism, Repeat, Measure, Same.
The average of repeated measurements, used to smooth individual variation.
